newsitem.title: USA: FEATURE-Saxophonist plays Chicago streets for inspiration.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE-Saxophonist plays Chicago streets for inspiration.

text.p: You might hear the familiar sounds of "Amazing Grace" teased out of a soprano saxophone as you walk out of a downtown commuter train station during the morning rush hour, or maybe a jazz-inflected "Greensleeves" outside the Art Institute of Chicago at lunchtime.

But, more likely than not, you will not be able to recognise the jazzy-bluesy tune Byard Lancaster is blowing because it will be his own composition. "The majority of the time I prefer to play my own melodies because I'm trying to research the response of the people," the 54-year-old musician, author and teacher told Reuters in an interview.

"You can make more money playing the standards but I dedicate most of my time to playing my own melodies and changing the key and changing the rhythm so I can find out what really sparks the people," he said. "Not by their contributions but by their eyes."

Lancaster's musical life has been anything but standard, so it should come as no surprise that his playing habits are not standard either. Born and raised in Philadelphia, he got his first saxophone when he was 4-1/2 years old after having already learned to play the piano.
"All during school I would add other instruments," he said. "At the present time I perform on nine instruments."

He spent a few years at Boston's Berklee College of Music but learned more listening to masters such as fellow Philadelphian John Coltrane, Sunny Murray and Cannonball Adderly during jazz's heyday in the 1950's and 60's.
"Basically I learned most of my playing from talking to great players that I went to see constantly wherever they were playing," he said.

After attending Berklee he toured the world, stopping in hot European jazz centres such as Paris and Frankfurt. In addition to sax greats Coltrane and Ornette Coleman, he counts among the major influences on him legendary bluesman Johnny "Clyde" Copeland, who died on July 3 of heart problems after a heart transplant.

He classifies his own style of music as world beat, "with the understanding of influences around the world. I'm derived from blues, jazz and gospel," he said, but he claims to be equally at home with reggae, funk and classical.
He is also at home in the recording studio. He cut his first recording in 1965 and has not stopped, performing as a sideman on about 70 albums and as bandleader on 11 recordings.

"By being a great sideman I imagined I could become a great leader," he said, listing Copeland, Murray, Ronald Shannon Jackson and McCoy Tyner among the band leaders he has sat in with. Over the years, he has also jammed with some of the most well-known names in the jazz and blues worlds: Ornette Coleman, Art Blakey, Stanley Clarke and Memphis Slim.

But Lancaster still finds playing solo every day in front of potentially thousands of passersby among the most rewarding and inspirational aspects of his work, saying his streetcorner playing was the easiest way to build a following.

"I try to make contact, so when I do perform at local venues I will have an audience to draw from," he said. In addition to the "tip cup" for donations, he puts out fliers, posters, cassette tapes and compact discs of his music for people to pick up or buy.
The response has been so good that Lancaster is working on a new recording to be called "Street Sax" -- "the same melodies I play on the street."

He splits his time between Chicago and Philadelphia, where he teaches at the Philadelphia Clef Club for the Performing Arts and is a consultant for the John Coletrane Society. He also plays on the streets of Philadelphia.

But playing on the street is becoming more difficult as his schedule calls for more time in recording studios, practice sessions and club gigs. He is working on a compilation of duets and trios to be called "Born Class" on which he will play clarinet, flute and saxophone. And he plans to fit in some time with Funkadesi, a Chicago-based band that plays what he called "Indo-Afro-Carribean" music.

When those sessions are finished, Lancaster plans to bring his band, Sounds of Newest Africa, together to record an album and then take off on a solo world tour next year. Among the stops planned are places he has not seen in a long time, including France, Germany and Belgium, and he may pick up his horn and head for the streets.
